prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ for $x < 2$ and $f(x) = 3x - k$ for $x \ge 2$. For what value of $k$ does $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ exist?
hint: A two-sided limit exists only when the left piece and the right piece head to the same height. What does each piece approach at $x = 2$?

hints.text: A two-sided limit exists only when the left piece and the right piece head to the same height. What does each piece approach at $x = 2$?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $f(x) = x$ for $x < 2$ and $f(x) = x + k$ for $x \ge 2$. The left side heads to $2$ and the right side to $2 + k$, so matching them forces $k = 0$. Use the same method here.
The left piece heads to $2^2 + 1 = 5$ and the right piece heads to $3(2) - k = 6 - k$. Set these two heights equal and solve for $k$.
Solving $6 - k = 5$ gives $k = 1$, so the limit exists when $k = 1$.

explanation: From the left, where $x < 2$, the rule is $x^2 + 1$, and it heads to $4 + 1 = 5$.
From the right, where $x \ge 2$, the rule is $3x - k$, and it heads to $6 - k$.
A limit exists only when both sides agree, so $6 - k = 5$, which gives $k = 1$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check it with the fix in place
steps: With $k = 1$ the right piece is $3x - 1$, and at $x = 2$ it gives $5$.
The left piece also heads to $5$. The two graphs meet at $(2, 5)$ — no gap, no jump.
Any other $k$ would leave a jump of size $|k - 1|$ at $x = 2$.
